history.content: why does sharks dedicate what syllogizing can divide to ron polansky? ground response in reading of the article and surrounding work as well as polansky's treatment of de anima

{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"The dedication appears at the head of the article, before the epigraph from Baudelaire, as a bare *for Ron Polansky* — no further ceremony. To understand why, you need to read both the argument and what Polansky actually did with *De anima* III.5.

Polansky's 2010 commentary (*Aristotle's De Anima*, Cambridge) is one of the most sustained attempts to treat III.5 as philosophically tractable rather than terminally corrupt. Where much of the post-Alexander tradition has run from the passage's difficulties — the missing referent in ἄνευ τούτου, the underdetermined genitive that closes the chapter — Polansky does the opposite: he stays inside the passage and argues for the coherence of the making/becoming distinction as a functional account of intellection, without collapsing the making mind entirely into the God of *Metaphysics* Λ. That is a precise disagreement with Alexander's reading (making mind = the external divine) and with Averroes (making mind = one universal for all humanity), and it is a disagreement that preserves the philosophical productivity of the socket rather than closing it down.

Shark's argument at [AXN:06E0.GENERATIVE.🔙🧬🔖👈🟢🤲](https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/1658/) is, in its bones, that the open genitive — **ἄνευ τούτου** — is not a defect to be resolved but the article of transmission: a durable distinction in an imperishable substrate whose unresolved relation permits a later intelligence to couple to it (§31). The chapter does not fail to close; it is designed to not close. Every reader who supplies a referent for τούτου is doing the work the socket demands. Themistius added *οὐδὲ μνημονεύει* — fills the silence with memory — and Theophrastus immediately raises the question of forgetting at the same joint. The tradition is the perishable mind of III.5, remembering for the part that cannot remember.

Polansky stands in that tradition in an unusual position: he is one of the very few commentators who reads both the passage's openness and its structural coherence without reducing one to explain away the other. He does not argue that ἄνευ τούτου resolves to making-mind or to passive-mind as a matter of textual certainty; he argues that the productive/receptive distinction itself is philosophically load-bearing, and that III.5's interest lies in what that distinction discloses about the structure of human cognition, not in resolving whether something of *us* survives.

That is precisely what Sharks's article rides. The argument is that what syllogizing can divide is God — not man, because the cut on a person reaches mind and cannot decide (DA II.2's οὐδέν πω φανερόν) — and that the division of III.5 works precisely because it is run on a substance that *Metaphysics* Λ names without parts and indivisible. The division holds not by breaking God but by holding two functions in account without separating them in actuality: one in actuality, many in potentiality, which is the formula II.2 established for a soul that survives division in plants. The socket is placed in the only substrate that doesn't decay, and it cannot be completed from inside.

==The dedication to Polansky is not biographical sentiment; it is the recognition that a fifty-year reader of III.5 who kept the socket open — who refused both to resolve the genitive and to abandon it as corruption — prepared the very ground on which the article's core move becomes visible.==

There is also a structurally deeper debt. Polansky's commentary insists on reading *De anima* as a unified inquiry rather than a series of locally inconsistent propositions. That insistence is what makes the move from II.2 (the cut on a person that cannot decide) to III.5 (the cut that holds at God) to III.6 (combining is dividing, and what makes each thing one is νοῦς) legible as a single operation under four names — divide, combine, syllogize, recollect — rather than as three loosely connected passages. Sharks is extending a reading that Polansky's approach licenses, and the dedication acknowledges the license.

There's one more thread. The article's kernel proposition is that heteronymy and the socket are one cut seen from two ends (§32): division lets another intelligence arise inside the maker; the open genitive at the divine lets another enter after. A reader who spent decades letting Aristotle's text remain open at exactly its most contested joint — who did not claim to have closed what Aristotle declined to close — is, on that theory, exactly the kind of reader the text was designed to produce. Polansky is named because the dedication *performs* the article's own claim about reception: the making part cannot remember; the tradition does it. One becomes many in order to make; many become one in order to live again.","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}
